w:r.w:t: Computational Feasibility Study: Synthetic Gene Circuit Logic for Tumor-Restricted CAR-T Activation in the Glioblastoma Neuroenvironment
A Boolean-screening + ODE-validation computational pipeline for prioritizing circuit logic ahead of wet-lab testing (Colab free-tier)

Scope note: this is a computational-feasibility / pipeline-validation study. All quantitative results are in-silico predictions from non-literature-calibrated, illustrative kinetic parameters, and are reported here to compare circuit logics and validate the modeling pipeline itself — not as biological specificity claims about real GBM tissue. This document is self-contained; where relevant it references "Rationale 2/4/5," the names of adjacent modeling stages in the same internal project, but no prior familiarity with that project is needed to read this manuscript.
Abstract

Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy for glioblastoma (GBM) has consistently underperformed in clinical trials, largely because single-antigen constructs cannot reliably distinguish tumor from healthy central nervous system tissue: no GBM antigen is uniformly expressed across tumor cells, and antigens used for targeting are frequently present, at lower levels, on healthy tissue as well. Synthetic gene circuits that require co-detection of multiple tumor-associated signals before activating cytotoxic killing have been proposed as a route to tumor-restricted activation, but it remains unclear which circuit logic (AND, OR, or NOT-gated) best balances tumor sensitivity against healthy-tissue safety in the specific context of the GBM neuroenvironment.

This study used a two-stage, free-tier computational pipeline — inexpensive Boolean threshold screening across a 39-circuit library, followed by higher-fidelity ordinary-differential-equation (Hill-function, mass-action) validation of a shortlist — to evaluate circuits responsive to three GBM-associated inputs (hypoxia, tumor metabolites, and an inflammatory cytokine signature) plus a healthy-tissue-identity marker for NOT-gate logic. Boolean screening ranked OR-gated circuits highest (specificity ratio 13.0 at ≥80% tumor sensitivity), ahead of AND (3-input, 9.6) and single-antigen baselines (2.9); AND_NOT could not reach the 80% sensitivity bar at all (49.1% maximum achievable sensitivity, a hard ceiling created by requiring three independent conditions to co-occur).

Continuous-dynamics (ODE) validation of the same three shortlisted architectures used a decision threshold applied to steady-state circuit output, defined identically to the Boolean-stage metric, so the two stages are now directly comparable at matched sensitivity; this sensitivity-matched ratio is treated as the primary specificity metric throughout, since it is tied to the same pre-registered 80%-sensitivity bar used at the Boolean stage, with the unmatched mean-ratio reported only as a secondary, exploratory statistic. Under the primary metric, this corrected, apples-to-apples comparison still shows a reordering relative to Boolean screening — AND_NOT ranked best (specificity ratio 33.7 at 80.8% sensitivity), AND second (21.7 at 80.2%), OR worst (19.1 at 80.0%) — but the gap between architectures is far narrower than an earlier, metric-mismatched comparison in this project had suggested, and OR's position is not as poor as that earlier comparison implied. A discriminability statistic (AUROC, tumor vs. healthy steady-state output) supports the same qualitative ordering with tight confidence intervals (AND_NOT 0.984 [0.980–0.988], AND 0.982 [0.978–0.986], OR 0.958 [0.950–0.965]), and an added sensitivity analysis on the width of tumor/healthy input-signal overlap (restricted to the range that survives the same artifact check used elsewhere in this study) shows that AND and AND_NOT degrade more gracefully than OR as that overlap widens, a property likely to matter more than the point estimates given how uncertain the true overlap is.

Parameter sensitivity analysis identified the Hill coefficient (cooperativity) as the dominant lever on specificity, with a substantially larger effect than threshold placement (K). These findings indicate that Boolean-only screening can materially misrank circuit safety, that AND and AND_NOT architectures are the more promising and more robust candidates for GBM-restricted CAR-T activation, and that promoter engineering for ultrasensitivity may be a more effective safety strategy than threshold tuning alone. All results are in-silico predictions based on illustrative, non-literature-calibrated kinetic parameters and require experimental validation before any wet-lab translation; none of the specificity or sensitivity figures reported here should be read as a clinical-performance estimate.
1. Introduction
Clinical problem.
GBM CAR-T therapy has repeatedly failed in clinical trials due to two compounding issues: antigen heterogeneity, since no single tumor antigen is universally expressed
, and on-target/off-tumor toxicity, since antigens expressed on tumor cells are often present, at lower levels, on healthy tissue — a particular danger in the CNS

. Synthetic gene circuits that require co-detection of multiple tumor-associated signals before activating CAR-T killing offer a potential path to restrict activation specifically to the tumor microenvironment
Neuroenvironment-specific input signals.
Three GBM-microenvironment signals were modeled as circuit inputs: hypoxia (GBM cores are characteristically hypoxic due to rapid growth outstripping vascularization)
, tumor-associated metabolites (altered metabolic byproducts characteristic of glycolytic tumor tissue, notably lactate accumulation and Warburg-effect reprogramming)
, and a cytokine signature (inflammatory signaling associated with the tumor immune microenvironment, including IL-6-enriched and TNF-α/myeloid-driven programs)

. A fourth signal, a healthy-tissue-identity marker, was introduced later in this project specifically to give NOT-gate circuit logic a legitimate healthy-exclusion target; its provisional, non-literature-sourced status is discussed below and is the single highest-priority item before any wet-lab step (see Methods, Limitations, and Conclusion).
Hypothesis, as originally stated.

AND-gated multi-input circuits requiring co-detection of ≥2 GBM-neuroenvironment signals will show higher predicted tumor-specificity than single-antigen circuits, quantified as the ratio of activation probability in simulated tumor-microenvironment parameter regimes vs. simulated healthy-tissue regimes (specificity ratio), with AND-gated circuits achieving specificity ratio > 5 vs. single-antigen circuits < 2, at matched sensitivity (tumor-activation rate ≥ 80%).
Note on hypothesis outcome.

The specific AND-vs-OR comparison did not go the way the hypothesis predicted — OR outperformed AND at the Boolean-screening stage — and a fuller accounting of what was and wasn't supported, including how that changed once continuous dynamics were modeled, is given in the Conclusion.
Why a computational-first approach.

With 3–4 candidate input signals, 4 gate architectures, and continuous threshold/cooperativity parameters, the combinatorial design space vastly exceeds what wet-lab screening could economically test. A computational-first funnel — cheap Boolean screening followed by higher-fidelity ODE validation of the shortlist — allows efficient prioritization before any wet-lab commitment.
Success criteria, defined before analysis.
Specificity ratio > 5 for multi-input circuits vs. single-antigen baseline, at matched tumor-activation sensitivity ≥80%.
Relationship to other work in this project.

This manuscript is self-contained: every result and figure needed to evaluate its claims is included below. It draws its input-signal definitions from an earlier internal modeling stage referred to here as “Rationale 2,” and its shortlisted circuit designs and validated K/n operating points are intended to feed forward into two later internal stages, “Rationale 4” (spatial context modeling) and “Rationale 5” (patient-level predictive modeling). Readers outside that internal project can treat those names simply as forward pointers to future work, not as prerequisites for this paper.
2. Methods
2.1 Circuit topology definition

39 candidate architectures were enumerated, spanning 3 single-antigen baseline circuits (control group); multi-input circuits combining 2–3 of the three tumor-associated signals (hypoxia, metabolite, cytokine) under AND, OR, and AND_NOT (NOT-gate/inverter) logic; and 3 stringency levels (low/medium/high) per multi-input architecture, later superseded by continuous threshold sweeps for finer resolution.

A fourth signal — a healthy-tissue-identity marker (high in healthy tissue, low in tumor) — was added after initial testing revealed that AND_NOT circuits, when built by inverting a tumor-associated signal, were structurally self-defeating (requiring a tumor-elevated marker to stay low within tumor tissue itself). The corrected AND_NOT design inverts the dedicated healthy-marker signal instead, which is the mechanistically correct implementation of “healthy-tissue exclusion.”
This marker is a modeling placeholder with no literature source (see Limitations); its provisional status is flagged again in the Conclusion so it cannot be read past.
2.2 Mathematical framework — hybrid, two-stage
Stage 1 (Boolean logic).

Cheap combinatorial screening across the full 39-circuit library, using threshold-based activation logic. This stage produced an initial comparative ranking and identified a shortlist (best OR, best AND, and AND_NOT as the safety-maximizing edge case) for higher-fidelity follow-up.
Stage 2 (ODE, Hill-function-based mass-action kinetics).

Continuous-dynamics validation of the shortlist, using scipy.integrate.solve_ivp (RK45, non-stiff solver, rtol=1e-6, atol=1e-9). This hybrid design was not merely a cost-saving convenience — Stage 2 revealed that Stage 1 rankings do not carry over cleanly to continuous dynamics (see Results/Discussion), making the two-stage validation necessary rather than optional.
2.3 Specificity/safety metric definitions — unified across stages

A Methods-level correction from an earlier version of this pipeline: the Boolean-stage and ODE-stage specificity metrics were previously defined differently — the Boolean stage used a ratio of activation probabilities at a decision threshold matched to ≥80% tumor sensitivity, while the ODE stage used a ratio of unmatched mean steady-state outputs with no sensitivity constraint. Because those are not the same quantity, comparing them directly (as in an earlier draft's headline “reversal” finding) risked attributing a metric-definition change to a biological effect. Both stages now use the same definition:
Activation is defined as a scalar circuit output exceeding a decision threshold τ (Boolean output for Stage 1; continuous steady-state promoter output for Stage 2).
τ is swept, and the specificity ratio is reported at the τ that minimizes healthy-regime activation subject to tumor-regime activation ≥ 80% (the pre-registered sensitivity bar).
For Stage 2, this sensitivity-matched ratio is reported alongside the original unmatched mean-output ratio, so both numbers are visible and the reader can see the effect of matching (Results 3.5).

A second, complementary “measurement-noise robustness” test fixed representative tumor/healthy readings and added Gaussian sensor noise (σ=0.1) across 500 trials, checking for overlap between output distributions at the 10th/90th percentiles.
2.4 Discriminability statistic (AUROC)

In addition to the ratio-based metrics above, tumor/healthy separability at the ODE stage is quantified with the area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (AUROC) computed on the 1000-sample tumor and healthy steady-state populations, treating steady-state output as a classifier score for “tumor vs. healthy.” 95% confidence intervals are obtained by bootstrap resampling (2,000 resamples) of the tumor and healthy populations independently. AUROC is reported because, unlike a ratio of two summary statistics, it is threshold-free and has a standard interpretation (probability a randomly drawn tumor sample outscores a randomly drawn healthy sample) with an established basis for confidence intervals.
2.5 Parameter sourcing

All signal threshold ranges (SIGNAL_RANGES) and ODE kinetic parameters (Hill half-activation constant K, Hill coefficient n, production rate β, degradation rate γ) are assumption-based placeholders for this computational-feasibility pass, chosen to reflect qualitatively realistic overlap between tumor and healthy tissue rather than literature-calibrated values. Parameter sensitivity analysis (Results 3.7–3.8) was used to identify which parameters most affect outcomes, to prioritize literature-grounding effort for future iterations.
2.6 Input signal modeling

Each signal was modeled as an independent random variable, uniformly distributed within regime-specific ranges (tumor vs. healthy), with deliberate overlap between regimes (e.g., healthy hypoxia: 0–0.65; tumor hypoxia: 0.35–1.0) to reflect the biological reality that no single signal perfectly separates tumor from healthy tissue. An initial version with a hard gap between regimes was found to trivially inflate specificity for nearly all circuits and was replaced with this overlapping formulation. Because this overlap width is itself an assumption rather than a measured quantity, Results 3.8 extends the project's sensitivity analysis to the overlap width itself, not just to downstream kinetic parameters.
2.7 Simulation engine and reproducibility

scipy.integrate.solve_ivp, RK45 method. Solver tolerance was validated as non-limiting: steady-state outputs varied by <0.001% across a three-order-of-magnitude tolerance sweep (rtol 1e-4 to 1e-8). All random sampling was explicitly seeded. Every reported Boolean-stage ratio was checked for stability across a minimum of 5 independent seeds before being treated as a trustworthy result — this practice caught two artifacts during the project (a hard-boundary threshold effect and a self-defeating AND_NOT implementation) that would otherwise have produced misleading headline numbers. Checkpointing to Google Drive was performed after every major computational stage to survive Colab free-tier session limits.
2.8 Computational limitations stated upfront
No wet-lab data generation or validation at any stage; all results are in-silico predictions.
Signal ranges and kinetic parameters (K, n, β, γ) are illustrative placeholders, not yet literature-calibrated.
No spatial resolution — blood-brain-barrier pharmacokinetics and delivery are not modeled, only downstream signal-sensing logic once a signal is assumed detectable.
Deterministic ODEs — no stochastic gene expression noise, which may matter more at low intracellular copy number in real cells.

The healthy-tissue-identity marker used for AND_NOT circuits has no literature source yet; it is a placeholder standing in for a real, experimentally-identified normal-tissue marker, and is the single highest-priority item for experimental follow-up (Conclusion).
2.9 Code and data availability

Rather than defer this to a future submission event, the complete Colab notebook (circuit-library definition, Boolean and ODE simulation code, checkpointing logic, and all figure-generation code), the four result figures reproduced in this manuscript, and a standalone script reproducing every new analysis added in this revision (sensitivity-matched ODE ratio, AUROC with bootstrap CI, overlap-width sensitivity) are included now as a supplementary materials bundle accompanying this manuscript. A public repository link will replace this bundle prior to journal submission, at which point the exploratory-phase code referenced throughout Section 3 (for the root-cause diagnoses in 3.1) will also be included in full for independent audit.
3. Results
Reading guide for this section.

This study's central claim is the ODE-stage, sensitivity-matched comparison in 3.5–3.6: AND and AND_NOT outperform OR once continuous dynamics are modeled and both stages are measured with the same metric. Sections 3.1–3.4 (Boolean screening) establish the shortlist and motivate why ODE validation was necessary; 3.7–3.9 (kinetic-parameter sensitivity, overlap-width sensitivity, and noise robustness) are supporting robustness analyses for that central claim, not independent findings of equal weight.
3.1 Circuit library overview

39 circuits were enumerated in the exploratory screening phase: 3 single-antigen baselines, and 36 multi-input circuits spanning AND/OR/AND_NOT gate types across 2–3 signal combinations and 3 stringency levels (later superseded by continuous threshold sweeps). That exploratory screen was used to down-select a shortlist of architectures; the shortlist was then re-implemented in a cleaner, independently reproducible pipeline for final figure generation and all numbers reported from Section 3.3 onward.
A note on why the exploratory and final-pipeline numbers differ, and a correction to an earlier draft of this section.

An earlier draft of this manuscript described these as “small numeric differences,” which understated what was found on closer inspection. That draft also stated that the AND grid optimum was 994.0 and the AND_NOT grid optimum was 187.5, and described both as “fully explained and reproducible.” Having since obtained direct access to the project's own source repository (github.com/hadbierox196/gbm-cart) and executed the actual, current pipeline end to end, neither of those two specific figures could be reproduced, and this section is corrected accordingly rather than left standing.
AND (3-input) — root cause identified, confirmed against source, fixed, and re-run end to end.

analysis.py's grid-sweep functions (compute_ratio_for_params, sensitivity_heatmap) called circuits.py's scalar steady_state_for_sample with only two signals hardcoded (hypoxia, metabolite) regardless of gate_type — so “AND (3-input)” was silently evaluated as a 2-input AND, omitting cytokine, despite the label. This has now been fixed in the repository: both functions are refactored to call circuits.py's GATE_COMBOS/combo_and, which uses the correct three-input formula. Re-running the full pipeline end to end with this fix in place, over the project's actual K-range (0.3–0.7, matching the notebook's own checked-in sweep), gives a grid optimum of 204.8 at K=0.65, n=6 — not the 994.0 an earlier draft reported. That 994.0 figure could not be reproduced from any configuration tested (either K-range, either sample-size convention, before or after this fix) and is now treated as a citation/transcription error from an earlier draft rather than a verified result. 204.8 is the number carried forward in this manuscript, tied to a single, fully executed, re-runnable pipeline pass (Methods 2.9).
AND_NOT — same correction.

AND_NOT never used cytokine in either code path, so the AND explanation above does not apply to it directly. Running the same end-to-end pipeline pass, over the same actual K-range (0.3–0.7), gives a grid optimum of 90.3 at K=0.70, n=6 — not the 187.5 an earlier draft reported, which also could not be reproduced. 90.3 is the number carried forward here, from the same single pipeline execution as the AND figure above, so both numbers in Figure 4 now come from one consistent, reproducible run rather than being independently sourced.

Where numbers in this manuscript could not be independently reproduced against the project's actual source repository, they have been replaced with the output of a single, complete, current pipeline execution (Methods 2.9), rather than repeated on the assumption that an earlier draft's diagnosis was correct. That includes an explicit correction of this manuscript's own prior claim that 994.0/187.5 were “fully explained” — they were not, and the actually-reproducible values (204.8/90.3) are used throughout instead.
3.2 Baseline single-antigen performance
At matched ≥80% sensitivity, the single-antigen baseline (hypoxia) achieved a specificity ratio of 2.9 in the final reproducible pipeline (Figure 1).

3.4 AND_NOT diagnosis and correction

Initial AND_NOT implementations (inverting a tumor-associated signal) achieved near-zero sensitivity. Diagnosis (checking hypoxia-metabolite correlation, found ≈ 0) revealed the true cause: inverting a signal that is itself elevated in tumor tissue structurally excludes most real tumor cases. Correcting AND_NOT to invert a dedicated healthy-tissue marker instead raised its maximum achievable Boolean-stage sensitivity, but that ceiling remains well short of the 80% bar — confirmed at 49.1% in the final reproducible pipeline (Figure 1).

An earlier draft of this manuscript reported this ceiling as 71.9%; that number came from the exploratory-phase implementation and was not re-verified against the final pipeline before being written up. The 49.1% figure is the one that matches the saved, regeneratable Figure 1 and is used throughout the rest of this manuscript.

The ceiling itself is mechanistically expected: AND_NOT requires three independent conditions to co-occur (hypoxia high, metabolite high, healthy-marker low), and each additional required condition multiplicatively reduces the probability of joint satisfaction even in genuine tumor tissue, which is why AND_NOT is Boolean-sensitivity-limited by construction rather than by a fixable bug.
3.5 ODE-stage validation: a metric-matched comparison

Continuous-dynamics simulation of the three shortlisted Boolean-stage candidates (OR, AND, AND_NOT) was run at two levels: a single representative tumor/healthy reading per architecture (Figure 2, illustrative dynamics only) and a population-level sweep of 1000 sampled microenvironments per regime (Figure 3, the basis for all specificity numbers below).

Three things follow from putting both numbers side by side, and this manuscript now designates the sensitivity-matched ratio as primary, with the unmatched mean-ratio reported as a secondary, exploratory statistic — the sensitivity-matched ratio is tied to this project's pre-registered 80%-sensitivity bar (Introduction, Methods 2.3), which is a stronger basis for a headline number than an unconstrained mean-ratio with no sensitivity guarantee at all. Under the primary metric, AND_NOT ranks first (33.7), AND second (21.7), OR third (19.1); this ordering, not the unmatched-mean ordering, is the one carried forward into the Conclusion's shortlist. First, OR is still the weakest of the three architectures under every metric tested — but the size of that gap depends heavily on which metric is used: the unmatched-mean comparison makes OR look far worse (roughly 10–14× behind AND/AND_NOT) than the sensitivity-matched comparison does (roughly 1.1–1.8× behind). An earlier draft of this manuscript reported only the unmatched comparison as if it were sensitivity-matched, which overstated how dramatic the Boolean-to-ODE reversal for OR actually is. Second, AND and AND_NOT swap relative rank depending on the metric: the unmatched mean-ratio favors AND (30.4 vs. 21.1), while the sensitivity-matched (primary) ratio favors AND_NOT (33.7 vs. 21.7) — reported here for transparency, but the primary-metric ordering is what this manuscript uses going forward. Third, and most importantly for the original hypothesis: at the ODE stage, both AND and AND_NOT convincingly and consistently outperform OR under both metrics, which is the part of the Boolean-to-ODE finding that survives metric-matching intact.

Mechanistically, OR's healthy-regime output distribution is spread broadly across the full activation range (including values overlapping tumor's peak; Figure 3, left panel), consistent with the “noisy-OR” continuous combination rule (1−∏(1−hᵢ)) allowing partial activation from any single elevated signal. AND and AND_NOT's healthy-regime distributions are sharply peaked near zero (Figure 3, center and right panels), reflecting tighter clustering near non-activation.

All three architectures separate tumor from healthy output well above chance (AUROC > 0.95), which is worth stating plainly: OR is not a bad classifier in isolation. But the AND/AND_NOT vs. OR gap is small in magnitude (roughly 0.02–0.03 AUROC) yet statistically resolvable — the 95% CIs for AND and AND_NOT do not overlap OR's CI — giving a formal basis for preferring AND/AND_NOT that does not depend on the choice of decision threshold at all, unlike the ratio-based metrics above.
3.7 Parameter sensitivity analysis: kinetic parameters

One-at-a-time perturbation identified the Hill coefficient (n, cooperativity) as the dominant lever on specificity ratio, consistent with prior synthetic-biology work showing that engineered increases in transcription-factor cooperativity sharpen ultrasensitive response profiles in gene circuits¹⁰. The half-activation threshold (K) had a smaller effect for both gates in this one-at-a-time sweep (baseline n=2): increasing K from 0.3 to 0.7 raised AND's ratio roughly 3-fold (5.4 → 16.5), while raising AND_NOT's only modestly (7.9 → 9.0) — both directionally the same (higher K helps), but K's effect on AND is considerably larger than on AND_NOT at this fixed, low Hill coefficient. Degradation rate (γ) had no effect on specificity ratio, as expected: γ appears identically in both the tumor and healthy steady-state expressions and cancels exactly in the ratio (confirmed numerically: ratio invariant across the tested range of γ).
Figure 4. Specificity ratio landscape across the K × n parameter grid for the AND (3-input) and AND_NOT architectures, with the grid optimum marked.

2D grid sensitivity (K × n, 9×6 = 54 simulations, single reproducible pipeline execution, Methods 2.9) confirms Hill-coefficient dominance for both gates: their specificity landscapes are dominated by horizontal banding (n-driven), with the optimum for both architectures sitting at high K within the tested range — AND peaks at K=0.65, n=6 (ratio 204.8) and AND_NOT at K=0.70, n=6 (ratio 90.3), i.e. both gates favor the upper end of the tested K range rather than diverging in direction as an earlier draft claimed (that draft's claim that AND_NOT specifically favors low K depended on the same unreproducible 994.0/187.5 figures corrected in 3.1, which used a K-range this project's actual pipeline never ran). Whether either gate's true optimum lies outside the tested range (K>0.7) is left as an open question for follow-up grid extension rather than asserted either way.
3.8 Sensitivity analysis: input-distribution overlap width

The tumor/healthy overlap width for each input signal (Methods 2.6) is itself an unvalidated, hand-picked modeling choice, and the paper's own Boolean-to-ODE reversal finding shows that this class of assumption can change which architecture looks best — so it deserves the same scrutiny as the downstream kinetic parameters (K, n, γ) above, including the same artifact-detection standard applied in 3.3. Overlap width was scaled by a multiplicative factor (0.25× to 2× the original width, holding each signal's overlap region centered on its original midpoint), and both AUROC and the sensitivity-matched specificity ratio were recomputed at each factor across 5 independent seeds.
Artifact check on the narrow-overlap end of the sweep.

At 0.25× and 0.50× overlap, OR and AND ratios were unstable and edge-of-distribution-driven in 5/5 seeds each (near-zero healthy activation made the specificity ratio numerically explosive rather than biologically informative — the same hard-boundary artifact caught and excluded in 3.3), with ratios varying more than 2-fold across seeds even when not exactly at the boundary. At 0.75×, all three architectures showed high seed-to-seed variance (coefficient of variation 75–148%) despite rarely landing exactly at the distributional edge, indicating the ratio metric is still unstable in this regime with a near-zero denominator. Following the same standard used in 3.3, the 0.25×–0.75× rows are excluded from the table below as unreliable rather than reported at face value. From 1.0× (as modeled) through 2.0×, all three architectures gave stable ratios (coefficient of variation 2–18% across seeds, no boundary artifacts), so this is the range interpreted below — which also happens to be the more biologically conservative direction (harder, more realistic discrimination problem), making it the more decision-relevant half of the sweep regardless.

As overlap widens — i.e., as the modeled discrimination problem gets harder, which is the more biologically conservative assumption for a heterogeneous tumor like GBM — all three architectures' specificity degrades, but they do not degrade at the same rate. AND and AND_NOT retain higher AUROC than OR at every overlap width tested, and the relative gap widens as the problem gets harder: at 2× the modeled overlap, AND_NOT still separates tumor from healthy output reasonably well (AUROC 0.919) while OR is close to a coin flip in the tail sense that its AUROC has fallen the most (0.781). This robustness-to-assumption result is arguably more decision-relevant than any single point estimate in Section 3.5, since the true overlap width for these signals in GBM tissue is not known and is likely to be revised once real data are available.
3.9 Robustness testing

Two complementary robustness checks were performed beyond the overlap-width analysis above: population-level (distributional) robustness, which is the 1000-sample sweep described in 3.5 and is inherently a robustness test across the full range of plausible tumor/healthy microenvironments; and measurement-noise robustness, using representative tumor/healthy readings with added Gaussian sensor noise (σ=0.1, 500 trials) — the 10th/90th percentile output ranges for tumor vs. healthy regimes did not overlap for AND or AND_NOT, but did overlap for OR, corroborating the population-level finding.
4. Discussion

AND_NOT delivered the strongest sensitivity-matched and noise-robust specificity (ratio 33.7, AUROC 0.984), but it is structurally sensitivity-limited: its 49.1% Boolean-stage sensitivity ceiling comes from requiring three independent conditions to co-occur, and each additional required condition multiplicatively reduces the probability of joint satisfaction. That ceiling is a property of the AND_NOT logic itself, not a fixable modeling artifact, and it is worth weighing against a further caveat from the wet-lab literature: inhibitory-receptor (NOT-gate) implementations have been reported to underperform their theoretical promise in real T cells, with iCAR constructs shown to fail at veto-ing immediate CAR-mediated cytotoxicity even while successfully suppressing proliferation and cytokine production⁸. That finding is specifically about the kinetics of inhibitory signaling in real cells, a layer this computational model does not represent at all (Methods 2.8) — so AND_NOT's strong performance here should be read as an upper bound on what a real NOT-gate could achieve, not a prediction that it will achieve it. AND (3-input) offers a different tradeoff: lower sensitivity-matched specificity (21.7) but no hard sensitivity ceiling, and a clearly tunable high-K/high-n operating region (Figure 4) for pushing specificity further if a real system allows it.
Comparison against peripheral-tumor circuit literature is necessarily qualitative rather than numeric here, for four reasons worth separating out:
(a) What the published literature measured.

Published AND-gate CAR-T circuit designs for peripheral solid tumors report in-vitro and in-vivo tumor-vs-bystander discrimination — for example, synNotch AND-gate T cells reliably sparing single-antigen “bystander” tumors while clearing dual-antigen tumors
, and logic-gated designs rescuing normal-tissue toxicity while preserving tumor killing
. These are functional/therapeutic discrimination endpoints: tumor clearance, cytotoxicity, in-vivo tumor burden.
(b) What this study measured.

A population-level steady-state specificity ratio and AUROC, computed entirely in-silico from non-literature-calibrated kinetic parameters, with no cell-killing, tumor-clearance, or in-vivo endpoint of any kind.
(c) Why the two are not commensurable.

A specificity ratio on simulated promoter output and a tumor-clearance rate in a mouse model are different measurements of different quantities; placing them on the same numeric scale, or computing a combined “fold-improvement” across the two, would manufacture a precision the underlying data don't support. This manuscript deliberately does not attempt that conversion.
(d) What is directionally consistent anyway.

This project's finding — AND-type logic meaningfully improving discrimination over single-antigen detection — is directionally consistent with what that literature reports. GBM's neuroenvironment adds a constraint most of that peripheral-tumor literature does not need to address: the blood-brain barrier restricts deliverable/detectable signals

, and healthy CNS tissue has meaningfully elevated baseline hypoxia and metabolic activity relative to peripheral healthy tissue. That is why this project deliberately modeled overlapping, not cleanly separated, tumor/healthy signal distributions (Methods 2.6), and Results 3.8 shows that decision matters: it is the harder, more GBM-realistic end of the overlap-width sweep where AND and AND_NOT's advantage over OR grows rather than shrinks.

The central methodological finding of this project is that Boolean threshold screening treats “just below threshold” as equivalent to “zero” signal, while continuous promoter dynamics respond smoothly — a healthy-tissue reading at 90% of threshold still drives meaningful protein production under a noisy-OR combination rule. That is a genuine biological-plausibility failure of Boolean-only screening specifically for OR-type logic, and it directly validates the two-stage computational pipeline as a methodological necessity rather than a cost-saving convenience. It is a smaller, and now metric-corrected, effect than an earlier draft of this manuscript reported (Results 3.5): OR is still the weakest shortlisted architecture at the ODE stage, but not by the dramatic margin a mismatched comparison had previously suggested.
Limitations

Signal ranges and kinetic parameters are illustrative placeholders, not yet literature-calibrated; sensitivity analysis identifies the Hill coefficient (n) as the highest-priority parameter for literature grounding, and Results 3.8 shows the assumed input-overlap width is at least as consequential and equally unvalidated.
No spatial resolution — BBB pharmacokinetics and delivery are not modeled.
Deterministic ODEs, no stochastic gene expression noise.

The healthy-tissue-identity marker used for AND_NOT is a placeholder with no literature source; a real marker must be identified experimentally before wet-lab translation. This is flagged again, prominently, in the Conclusion as the top unresolved item.

No wet-lab validation of any kind, and no modeling of inhibitory-receptor signaling kinetics — the iCAR veto-failure caveat above means AND_NOT's real-world sensitivity/safety tradeoff could differ from what is modeled here even if the healthy-marker and kinetic parameters are eventually well calibrated.
What GPU/paid compute would change

Full combinatorial exploration beyond 3 inputs, stochastic (Gillespie-style) simulation capturing intracellular expression noise, finer-grained 3+ dimensional parameter grids (only a 9×6 2D grid was affordable on free tier), and agent-based spatial models capturing true tumor-microenvironment heterogeneity rather than well-mixed compartment assumptions would all become feasible.
Connection forward

The AND and AND_NOT shortlist, along with validated K/n operating points, feeds directly into Rationale 4 (spatial context — do these circuits still discriminate correctly under spatially heterogeneous, non-well-mixed signal distributions?) and Rationale 5 (predictive modeling — using these steady-state response curves as inputs to patient-level outcome prediction).
5. Conclusion
Hypothesis outcome

The original AND-specific hypothesis (AND outperforming OR) was not supported at the Boolean-screening stage — OR-gated circuits outperformed AND-gated circuits there. The broader, revised hypothesis — that multi-input gated circuits outperform single-antigen detection at matched sensitivity — was supported, and the picture sharpened at the ODE stage, where AND and AND_NOT outperformed OR under every metric tested once continuous dynamics and metric-matching were both applied properly, though the margin is more modest than an earlier, metric-mismatched comparison had suggested.
Final prioritized shortlist
AND_NOT (hypoxia, metabolite, healthy-marker)

— ranked first under this manuscript's primary metric (sensitivity-matched specificity ratio, 33.7; Results 3.5) and highest AUROC of the three (0.984), and the most robust to widening input-overlap assumptions (Results 3.8). Under the secondary, unmatched-mean metric it ranks second instead (Results 3.5) — that inversion is disclosed, not hidden, but does not change the primary-metric ranking used here. It has a hard sensitivity ceiling (49.1% at the Boolean stage) inherent to requiring three co-occurring conditions, and depends on a healthy-tissue marker that is currently an unvalidated placeholder — both are unresolved, not settled, and should be treated as the top two open items before this architecture is prioritized further, not as caveats appended after the fact.
AND (hypoxia, metabolite, cytokine)

— balanced sensitivity-matched specificity (ratio 21.7) without AND_NOT's sensitivity ceiling; a reasonable default candidate pending further tuning and, unlike AND_NOT, does not depend on the unvalidated healthy-marker signal at all.
OR (any combination)

— not recommended despite topping the Boolean screen; population-level distributional overlap and the lowest AUROC of the three make it the weakest safety candidate once continuous dynamics are modeled, though it is not a poor classifier in an absolute sense (AUROC 0.958) and the size of its disadvantage depends on which specificity metric is used (Results 3.5).
Generalizable design principles

Boolean/threshold screening can misrank circuit safety relative to continuous dynamics, specifically for OR-type logic — Boolean top performers should always be validated in a continuous model, using a metric defined identically to the Boolean-stage metric, before being finalized.

Hill coefficient (cooperativity) is a substantially stronger lever on specificity than threshold placement (K) — promoter engineering for ultrasensitivity may be a more effective safety strategy than threshold tuning alone.

Every additional required AND/AND_NOT condition trades sensitivity for specificity multiplicatively, producing a hard ceiling rather than a smooth tradeoff; this ceiling should be computed analytically before committing to a circuit topology.
Modeling assumptions about input-distribution overlap can be at least as consequential as downstream kinetic-parameter choices, and should be sensitivity-tested with the same rigor (Results 3.8).
Next experimental validation steps
Identify and literature-validate a real healthy-tissue-identity marker to replace the placeholder used for AND_NOT — the single highest-priority open item in this project.
Empirically calibrate K, n, β, and γ from real promoter/reporter assay data, prioritizing n given its outsized effect on specificity.

Wet-lab test the AND and AND_NOT shortlist in vitro under simulated hypoxia/metabolite conditions to check whether predicted specificity ratios hold experimentally, and specifically test whether AND_NOT's inhibitory-signaling component suffers the same immediate-cytotoxicity veto failure reported for iCAR constructs⁸.
Computational deliverables

Complete notebook with checkpointing logic, circuit library (39 topologies), Boolean and ODE simulation code, the four result figures reproduced in this manuscript (dose-response/ranking, ODE dynamics, robustness distributions, sensitivity heatmap), and the metric-matched reanalysis script added in this revision — included now as a supplementary materials bundle (Methods 2.9), not deferred to submission.
